title: How he plays lead and the last chorus
summary: He describes ensemble and chorus order, varying the last chorus, and playing alone at home.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, that's another thing. How do you feel about, uh, when you're playing there in the ensemble, do you, what kind of lead do you think you should play in the ensemble? How do you aim to play?

Well, that's a, that's a, uh, quite question and answer. Yeah, I know. I just play the way I feel. I take off in a tempo and that's it. And I try to set that drive until the, the, the piece is kicked out.
Well, say how many choruses do you play, the first ensemble?

Well, generally if it's a, if it's just a piece that you're going to play only choruses, you kick off, you, the whole group will play the first chorus. After the first chorus you let the clarinet man take it for a chorus. Let the trombone man take the next chorus, piano man take the next, about five, five choruses, six choruses, and then on the last chorus you won't go out. Or sometimes you take two, you know. If you're going real good you might kick it off to one more, you know. It all depends how you feel. If the piece is, is clicking nice you go, extra chorus.
Well that extra chorus, do you play it any different from the one before?

Oh yeah, you really break that last one down man. Like I was playing, last night I was playing my one, what you think I was, the wang wang blues. And man I was just playing some, some parts in there that I really liked to have been playing with a band. To, to make what I had in my mind when I was playing, you know. I knew it would fit right in, you know, for, for the last kick out chorus. I was just sitting down there toot my horn to myself. I often do it, sit my paw by myself.
Well do you, uh, play the melody straight on the last chorus or do you vary the little?

Oh you vary, yeah, you make variations in there. But, uh, I, I always like to stick to the melody so everybody knows what you're playing, Dick. I was sitting in my, Paula the other day playing, who you think walks in there? Yeah. He says, look at all this talent going to work. It's Butch Massico. He's, uh, you know Butch, the drummer?
Yeah, I've seen him. He plays, he works for this Orkin people.

They spray, they spray our house. And he says, ah, what, you don't play no more. I said, no, boy. I said, man, you oughta get what I do. I was playing the Tin Roof Blues when he walked in. He said, you're letting all this talent go to waste. Is he that sort of tall, skinny guy? Nice guy. Yeah. Used to play with Kelton for, oh, he played in a blue room with Kelton for years. He's a nice guy. I heard him. I heard him.
